cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Government & the Constitution
cards.back: The Republic was a mixed constitution with monarchical (consuls), aristocratic (Senate) and democratic (assemblies) elements

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Government & the Constitution
cards.back: Two consuls were elected annually with imperium (power of command); they could veto each other (intercessio)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Government & the Constitution
cards.back: The Senate was the most powerful body: 300 patrician elders who controlled foreign policy, finances and state religion

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Government & the Constitution
cards.back: The comitia centuriata (centuriate assembly) elected consuls and declared war; voting was weighted by wealth

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Government & the Constitution
cards.back: Tribunes of the plebs (10 annually elected plebeian officers) could veto any magistrate's action and summon the Senate

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Government & the Constitution
cards.back: In emergencies, a dictator could be appointed for six months with supreme power

cards.front: What should you know about gcse ancient history exam tips — roman government & the constitution?
cards.back: 1. For Roman Government & the Constitution, include specific factual detail: dates, names, events and statistics where relevant 2. For source questions, analyse provenance (who, when, why, audience) before using the content 3. In evaluation questions, discuss multiple factors and weigh their relative significance 4. Always link back to the question focus — don't just narrate what happened with Roman Government & the Constitution 5. Use phrases like 'the most significant factor was... because...' to show analytical judgement
